title: The End of Bigfoot? New Evidence May Finally Expose the World's Most Famous Sighting as a Hoax
excerpt: New footage threatens a decades-old legend that shaped lives, divided families, and defied scientific scrutiny.
content:
For nearly 60 years, one grainy film has kept the legend of Bigfoot alive. Now, a second reel may show that “Bigfoot” was just a man in a suit, following a script.

The grainy, 59-second film, shot in a California forest in 1967, became the closest thing Bigfoot believers ever had to a smoking gun. It launched decades of investigations, inspired countless expeditions, and convinced generations that something extraordinary was hiding in the woods.

Now, a new documentary claims to have finally cracked the case. Capturing Bigfoot, directed by Marq Evans, presents previously unseen (and clearer) footage that appears to show a dress rehearsal for the legendary encounter, along with testimony from the original filmmaker’s family and the man who says he played the Bigfoot. In perhaps the most remarkable revelation, both the filmmaker’s son and widow have reportedly acknowledged that the original footage was a hoax.

The obsession

Long before he supposedly captured Bigfoot on camera, Roger Patterson was obsessed with finding it.

A rodeo cowboy and amateur filmmaker from Yakima, Washington, Patterson became fascinated with reports of enormous, humanlike creatures roaming the forests of the Pacific Northwest. He collected eyewitness accounts, investigated mysterious footprints and cast them with plaster, and in 1966 even published a book titled Do Abominable Snowmen of America Really Exist?

But Patterson wanted to capture the creature on film.

He enlisted friends and acquaintances in his pursuit, including fellow cowboy Bob Gimlin, whom he persuaded to join expeditions into the wilderness. Gimlin was initially skeptical, but Patterson’s enthusiasm proved infectious.

But despite the enthusiasm, Patterson was running out of money. He turned to his brother-in-law, Al DeAtley, who ran a construction company called Superior Asphalt. DeAtley helped finance the venture, although he shared little of Patterson’s fascination with the creature.

×

Patterson and his new crew started working on a movie about men hunting Bigfoot. In the spring of 1967, he recruited several acquaintances to act in scenes for the unfinished production. Among them was Bob Heironimus, a young man from the Yakima area who would later make an extraordinary claim: that he had worn the costume in Patterson’s famous footage.

According to Heironimus, Patterson and Gimlin recruited him to impersonate Bigfoot, promising him $1,000 (approximately $10,100 in 2026 money) for his participation. He says he never received the money.

On October 20, 1967, Patterson and Gimlin said they finally encountered the creature near Bluff Creek in Northern California.

A large, hairy figure was striding across a clearing. The creature, later nicknamed “Patty,” briefly turned toward the camera before disappearing into the trees.

Those 59 seconds became legendary. Skeptics saw a man in a suit. But believers scrutinized Patty’s unusually long arms, heavy build, and distinctive gait, arguing that no human could convincingly move that way inside a costume.

Patterson, who died in 1972, maintained that the reel was genuine. So did Gimlin. For decades, the argument went nowhere.

But it turns out, there was another shot.

The second reel

For decades, a mysterious 16-millimeter reel sat locked inside a safe belonging to Norm Johnson, who ran a film department at Boeing in Washington during the 1960s. Johnson’s brother, Dave, reportedly knew Patterson, and family accounts suggested that the brothers had been involved in producing or processing footage connected to the Bigfoot film.

In 2022, Johnson’s daughter, Teresa Brooks, an instructor at Olympic College, contacted filmmaker Marq Evans, who taught at the same institution. She wanted to know what was on the old reel.

Evans arranged to have it digitally scanned, and he was stunned. This wasn’t the famous Patterson–Gimlin film, but something even more interesting.

The footage showed a different-looking Bigfoot figure walking through the woods, apparently following the same choreography as Patty. Like the creature in the celebrated film, it turned its head toward the camera at a suspiciously convenient moment.

According to the Los Angeles Times, the newly discovered film is believed to date to 1966, a year before Patterson’s famous encounter. Evans suspects it was an early attempt that Patterson subsequently improved, modifying the costume and possibly replacing the performer.

Patterson’s nephew Vaile Thompson says the figure in the earlier footage looks like DeAtley, Patterson’s brother-in-law. According to Thompson, the group tried DeAtley in the costume but found that his walk looked too human. That is family testimony, not a verified identification.

In other words, it may have been a dress rehearsal for one of history’s most famous alleged Bigfoot encounter.

Some things are still unclear. The film-stock markings indicate a 1966 manufacturing date, although that alone cannot establish when the footage was shot. And the supposed rehearsal remains contested. Bigfoot-film researcher Bill Munns, who appears in the documentary, has challenged the filmmakers’ interpretation, arguing that the footage falls short of establishing a hoax.

Nevertheless, the discovery gives new weight to Heironimus’s longstanding account. In Capturing Bigfoot, he demonstrates the creature’s famous walk and describes being instructed to look back toward the camera.

Combined with the testimony of Patterson’s surviving family, the footage offers something skeptics have sought for decades: a possible explanation not only for what appears in the original film, but for how it was created.

The severe price of the truth

The film made Bigfoot a global household name. It also made Patterson a folk hero and created a valuable piece of footage that television programs could license for decades.

Patterson and DeAtley incorporated it into a theatrical presentation that toured auditoriums and movie theaters. DeAtley was its chief promoter. In an archival interview featured in the documentary, he recalled taking in $84,000 at one venue—around $850,000 in 2026.

After Patterson’s death, his widow, Patricia, inherited the rights and earned income from its continued circulation. Their son, Clint Patterson, inherited something more abstract: an obligation to live with his father’s story. Eventually, he came to believe the film was a hoax. When he wanted to speak publicly, the disagreement with his mother became so severe that they stopped talking for eight years.

“I paid a severe price for telling the truth,” Clint told the Los Angeles Times in an interview. He recalled his father coming home with the extraordinary news that he had filmed Bigfoot, yet being unable to look his son in the eye.

But something has changed. Patricia herself now appears in the documentary, reportedly acknowledging that the famous encounter was staged. For a family that spent decades divided over the film, that represents a remarkable reversal.

Even so, Clint does not portray his father as a monster. “He has always been my hero,” he said. He wishes Patterson had found a different way to use his talents.

Evans originally planned a straightforward investigation into the film. Once Clint agreed to speak, the director realized the emotional consequences mattered as much as exposing a possible deception. The documentary also includes Patricia’s account and the reactions of people who dedicated decades to the mystery.

For Clint, breaking the silence meant challenging a story his mother had defended for years—and one that had helped support the family.

The money, rivalries, and competing versions of the truth strained families and destroyed friendships. Bigfoot was no longer just a mysterious creature supposedly hiding somewhere in the wilderness. For some, it had become a livelihood, a community, and a reason to keep searching.

The lack of proof

But even if the Patterson–Gimlin film was staged, that raises another question. What does science actually say about Bigfoot?

A hoax would not, by itself, disprove Bigfoot’s existence. Science can’t rule out every animal someone might imagine in an unexplored forest and it’s extremely hard to prove a negative. But science can, however, ask what evidence should exist if a breeding population of giant primates had been roaming North America for generations.

There should be remains, teeth, bones, reliably documented sightings or biological traces that independent investigators can identify. Despite countless reports, no verified Bigfoot specimen has emerged.

Genetic testing has produced particularly sobering results. In a 2014 study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, researchers examined 37 hair samples associated with alleged Bigfoot, Yeti, and other mysterious primates. Of these, 30 yielded usable DNA sequences, which matched known mammals, including bears, horses, cattle, and other familiar animals. None provided evidence of an unknown giant ape.

The results cannot establish that every alleged Bigfoot sample is misidentified, but they illustrate how often an extraordinary claim dissolves under ordinary laboratory scrutiny.

Some sightings may have ordinary wildlife behind them. A 2024 study in the Journal of Zoology found that areas with more American black bears also tended to report more Bigfoot sightings, even after accounting for human population and forest cover. The analysis cannot identify what any particular witness saw, but bears occasionally rear up and move on their hind legs.

Some Bigfoot enthusiasts have proposed a more exotic explanation: that the creature is a surviving descendant of Gigantopithecus blacki, the largest ape ever known to science. This giant primate lived in Asia, and some have speculated that its descendants crossed into North America via an ancient land bridge.

But there’s a major problem with the theory. A 2024 study in Nature found that Gigantopithecus likely went extinct between 295,000 and 215,000 years ago, after struggling to adapt to changing forests. Its fossils have never been found in North America. There’s no evidence that it survived, migrated across the Bering land bridge, or walked upright like Bigfoot supposedly does.

The famous film had always offered something specimens and DNA had not: an apparently visible creature. If that image was staged, the scientific case for Bigfoot becomes no stronger than it was before.

It’s about psychology, not biology

How could one minute of ambiguous film sustain nearly 60 years of belief? Part of the explanation may lie in how people perceive uncertainty.

Our brains constantly search for meaningful shapes and patterns. In ambiguous images, expectations can influence what we think we see. Once convinced, we may favor details supporting our interpretation while discounting evidence against it—a tendency psychologists call confirmation bias.

Researchers have examined related processes in people who endorse paranormal beliefs. A 2022 study in Consciousness and Cognition found that people who were more inclined to believe in the paranormal showed lower perceptual sensitivity when distinguishing meaningful visual signals from random noise.

It wasn’t a study of Bigfoot enthusiasts, and it cannot explain any particular person’s convictions. But it illustrates how ambiguous imagery may leave room for deeply different interpretations.

Belief also becomes harder to revise when it is entwined with identity. Some Bigfoot hunters have spent years defending the film, traveling to conferences and building friendships around the search. Accepting that Patty might have been an actor is not simply changing one’s mind about a movie. It can feel like repudiating a life’s work.

There may also be financial considerations. Bob Gimlin continues to stand by the authenticity of the 1967 encounter, even as Patterson’s family challenges the story. After years of avoiding the spotlight, Gimlin began attending Bigfoot conventions in 2003, becoming a celebrity within the community. The film became part of his public identity and a source of income. That creates a potential conflict of interest, although it tells us nothing definitive about the sincerity of his beliefs.

Evans acknowledged to the Los Angeles Times that admitting they were wrong can be especially difficult for people who have spent decades arguing over the film. He said he hoped to reach those who remained uncertain, rather than force committed believers to agree.

Is this the end of Bigfoot?

Not everyone who encounters the documentary’s evidence finds it liberating. Longtime Bigfoot investigator Larry Lund, for example, becomes emotional as he considers what the new footage could mean for the search that occupied so much of his life.

But there is a distinction between a false claim and a wasted life. The people who traveled together, explored remote valleys, and formed lasting friendships did those things, whatever appears in the 1967 film. The mystery supplied adventure and belonging, even if its most celebrated proof was manufactured.

For Clint Patterson, the reckoning has been more direct. Speaking publicly meant confronting his father’s legacy and reopening a painful family rift. Yet it also gave him something the film had denied him for decades: the freedom to tell his own story.

“Wow. What a relief it has been,” he told the Los Angeles Times.

Bigfoot reports will almost certainly continue. A single alleged hoax can’t settle every story told about a strange figure in the forest. But if the documentary’s central claim holds up, one of the most recognizable images in cryptozoology will have told us far more about human ingenuity—and human belief—than about an undiscovered animal.
